per_question.question: Who were the three astronauts on the Apollo 11 mission and what role did each play?
per_question.expected_answer: Neil Armstrong (Commander, first to walk on the Moon), Buzz Aldrin (Lunar Module Pilot, second to walk on the Moon), and Michael Collins (Command Module Pilot, remained in lunar orbit).
per_question.answer: The Apollo 11 crew was Neil A. Armstrong (Commander, CDR), Edwin E. "Buzz" Aldrin Jr. (Lunar Module Pilot, LMP), and Michael Collins (Command Module Pilot, CMP). Armstrong and Aldrin descended in the Lunar Module Eagle and walked on the lunar surface in the Sea of Tranquility, while Collins remained alone in lunar orbit aboard the Command Module Columbia, performing communications relay and rendezvous-tracking duties (Apollo 11, public affairs officer transcript and flight plan).

per_question.question: What problems did Apollo 13 encounter, and what was the cause?
per_question.expected_answer: An oxygen tank in the Service Module ruptured roughly 56 hours into the flight, causing a loss of electrical power, oxygen, and water in the Command Module. The crew used the Lunar Module as a lifeboat to return safely to Earth.
per_question.answer: Approximately 56 hours into the mission, immediately after Mission Control's request to "stir up your cryo tanks" (Apollo 13, technical transcript), an oxygen tank in the Service Module exploded. This caused the loss of one fuel cell, depletion of the second oxygen tank, and a sharp drop in Main Bus B voltage. Crippling losses of electrical power, breathing oxygen, and water followed in the Command Module Odyssey. The crew (Lovell, Swigert, Haise) powered down the Command Module and used the Lunar Module Aquarius as a lifeboat for life support, propulsion, and guidance during a free-return trajectory back to Earth (Apollo 13, technical + command-module transcripts).

per_question.question: What were the last communications between the Challenger crew and Mission Control before the disaster?
per_question.expected_answer: Routine ascent callouts: 'Roger, go at throttle up' acknowledged by Commander Dick Scobee. Loss of all data and voice communication occurred shortly after at approximately T+73 seconds.
per_question.answer: The final exchanges were routine ascent callouts. Public Affairs called "Challenger, go at throttle up" once the main engines returned to 104% thrust, which Commander Francis "Dick" Scobee acknowledged with "Roger, go at throttle up." Approximately 73 seconds after liftoff, all telemetry and voice from the Orbiter ceased and the vehicle broke apart (Challenger STS-51L, mission audio transcript). The transcripts in the archive cover countdown, ascent callouts, and the immediate post-loss-of-vehicle response by Launch Control.

per_question.question: Walk me through the timeline of Apollo 11 from launch to lunar landing.
per_question.expected_answer: Launch on 16 July 1969, translunar injection ~2h 44m after launch, lunar orbit insertion on 19 July, Eagle separation and powered descent on 20 July with touchdown in the Sea of Tranquility at 20:17 UTC.
per_question.answer: Apollo 11 launched from Pad 39A on 16 July 1969 at 13:32 UTC atop a Saturn V. After Earth-parking-orbit checks, the S-IVB performed Translunar Injection (TLI) about 2 hours 44 minutes after launch. Transposition, docking, and CSM-LM extraction followed. On 19 July the stack entered lunar orbit via the Lunar Orbit Insertion burn. On 20 July the Lunar Module Eagle undocked from Columbia and began Powered Descent Initiation; Eagle touched down in the Sea of Tranquility at approximately 20:17 UTC on 20 July 1969, with Armstrong's first step occurring later that day (Apollo 11, flight plan and technical transcript).

per_question.question: What technical procedures did the Apollo 13 crew use to conserve power in the Command Module?
per_question.expected_answer: They powered down the Command Module to a minimal state, transferred guidance information to the Lunar Module, used the LM's descent stage for propulsion and life support, and conserved water, oxygen, and battery power for the re-entry sequence.
per_question.answer: After the SM oxygen tank rupture, the crew performed an emergency power-down of the Command Module Odyssey: shutting non-essential buses, fuel cells, and inertial-platform heaters; transferring the IMU alignment via verbal angles to the Lunar Module Aquarius PGNCS; and stopping water dumping. The LM's descent stage provided life support (oxygen, lithium-hydroxide CO2 scrubbing — supplemented later by the CSM "mailbox" adapter) and propulsion (two PC+2 and one mid-course DPS burns on the free-return). Battery power in the CM was reserved exclusively for the final entry sequence: CM power-up roughly two hours before Entry Interface, with platform alignment, ECS reactivation, and pyrotechnic-arming on the Entry battery (Apollo 13, technical transcript; command-module transcript).

per_question.question: Give me a general overview of the Challenger mission STS-51L.
per_question.expected_answer: STS-51L was the 25th Space Shuttle mission and the 10th flight of the orbiter Challenger. It launched on 28 January 1986 and broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff due to a failure of an O-ring seal in the right Solid Rocket Booster, killing all seven crew members.
per_question.answer: STS-51L was the 25th Space Transportation System launch and the 10th flight of the orbiter Challenger, lifting off on 28 January 1986 at 16:38 UTC from Launch Complex 39B at the Kennedy Space Center (Challenger STS-51L mission audio). The seven-member crew was Commander Francis "Dick" Scobee, Pilot Michael Smith, Mission Specialists Judy Resnik, Ellison Onizuka, and Ronald McNair, Payload Specialist Greg Jarvis, and Teacher-in-Space participant Christa McAuliffe. The vehicle broke apart approximately 73 seconds after liftoff during ascent; all seven crew members were lost. The cause, established by the Rogers Commission, was a failure of the right Solid Rocket Booster's aft-field-joint O-ring seal in unusually cold launch-day conditions.
